editor_spans.body: The most important move in the Motherwell speech is a reframing, not a policy. Burnham says Scotland's problems are 'similar' to England's: the same cost-of-living pressure, the same gaps between regions, the same empty high streets. He also names Holyrood alongside Westminster as a centre that has failed to let go.

For a quarter-century Scottish politics has been argued along a Scotland-versus-England line. The speech tries to replace it with a line between places and centres, and on that line Edinburgh sits with London. Calling Scotland 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe' turns the nationalist complaint about distant power back on the Scottish Government.

The harder content sits in the offer itself. Employment support from the DWP has always been reserved to Westminster. Offering to devolve it, along with innovation and enterprise funding, is a real transfer of power. But it comes with conditions: it must follow the 'Easterhouse principle' and push power down to regions. The first venue is a National Economic Council that has not met under this Prime Minister. Edinburgh gets new powers only if it agrees not to keep them at Holyrood.

Ravenscraig is the right place for this argument, and it says more than Burnham does. When it closed, Britain lost more than a community. It also lost much of its capacity to make heavy things at scale.

The government now proposes to reindustrialise partly through defence: technical colleges funded with matched £10 million contributions, and support for shipbuilding. That is the same capacity whose absence limits how fast Britain can arm Ukraine.
The sums show how far there is to go. Two colleges and £10 million on each side are a start for a country that once supplied the steel for anything big it built.

The procurement passage is the most radical thing in the speech. Burnham says he chose Falkirk-built buses at a higher price and rejected 'the old Whitehall way' of the cheapest contract anywhere in the world. He wants all UK public procurement to work like that.

That runs against decades of Treasury value-for-money doctrine. It is also the policy most likely to collide with trade commitments and the department's own instincts. If it survives contact with the spending rules, it would matter more to places like Motherwell than any reorganisation of who sits on which regional board.
